title: AI-assisted IHC pre-screening: Benefits for pathologists
summary: Learn how AI-powered pre-screening helps pathology teams reduce IHC turnaround times, decrease unnecessary staining, and improve workflow efficiency while supporting diagnostic quality
body_markdown:
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) plays a critical role in cancer diagnostics, but it can also introduce delays into the pathology workflow. Every additional stain requires laboratory resources, pathologist review time and, ultimately, more time before clinicians and patients receive the results they need.


As pathology teams face increasing workloads and[ongoing workforce shortages](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/2026-pathology-staffing-cliff-why-digital-infrastructure-no-longer-optional) , many laboratories are exploring artificial intelligence (AI) as a way to streamline workflows without compromising diagnostic quality. One promising application is AI-powered pre-screening, which helps identify cases that are likely negative while prioritizing suspicious findings for faster review and additional testing.


**Why IHC turnaround time remains a challenge**


In a traditional workflow, a pathologist first reviews an H&E-stained slide and then determines whether IHC testing is needed. Cases requiring additional staining must move through another processing cycle before returning to the pathologist for final interpretation. This sequential approach can slow turnaround times, especially in high-volume laboratories.


The impact extends beyond laboratory operations. Delays in biomarker results can postpone treatment decisions, particularly in cancers where markers such as HER2, ER/PR, PD-L1 or MMR status help guide therapy selection. Faster access to clinically actionable information can help support more timely care.


**How AI pre-screening works**


AI pre-screening applies deep learning algorithms to digitized H&E whole-slide images before a pathologist reviews the case. After analyzing tissue morphology, the system assigns a confidence score and routes the case into one of three categories:


- **Likely negative cases** , which can be reviewed and cleared more efficiently
- **Likely positive cases** , which can be prioritized for immediate pathologist evaluation and, in some workflows, trigger earlier IHC ordering
- **Indeterminate cases** , which proceed through standard expert review


Rather than replacing the pathologist, AI serves as a workflow orchestration tool that helps focus attention where it is needed most.


**What the evidence shows**


Recent clinical studies suggest that AI-assisted pre-screening can deliver meaningful improvements in both efficiency and resource utilization.


In[prostate cancer workflows](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42245328/) , investigators reported a 30% reduction in diagnostic turnaround time and a 38% decrease in IHC utilization following AI implementation. The model maintained high sensitivity and specificity, demonstrating that efficiency gains did not come at the expense of diagnostic performance.


Similarly, a[breast cancer study evaluating an AI-assisted workflow](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07060599) found a 41% reduction in diagnostic review time and a 40% reduction in IHC testing. Researchers also observed improvements in sensitivity and pathologist confidence when AI was incorporated into the review process.


Across studies,[AI-assisted workflows](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12785249/) have also been associated with measurable time savings for pathologists, helping relieve pressure on increasingly constrained pathology teams.


**How AI helps reduce unnecessary staining**


One of the most significant opportunities lies in identifying cases that are unlikely to require additional testing.


Many AI models can detect subtle morphological patterns within routine H&E slides and identify specimens that have a very low probability of containing clinically significant findings. When validated thresholds are met, these cases can move through the workflow more efficiently while reserving IHC resources for cases that genuinely require further investigation.


[Several emerging algorithms](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12317095/) can also predict biomarker status directly from H&E images, opening the door to more targeted IHC ordering strategies. While these technologies continue to evolve, they highlight[how AI could further reduce unnecessary staining](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-26122-w) and associated costs in the future.


**Safety remains a critical requirement**


The success of AI pre-screening depends on maintaining diagnostic safety.


Most clinical AI systems are intentionally designed with extremely high sensitivity and negative predictive value, meaning they are more likely to flag uncertain cases than mistakenly clear a positive one. Importantly, current implementations still require pathologist review and final sign-off. AI supports decision-making and workflow prioritization, but it does not function as an autonomous diagnostic tool.


Research consistently shows that[the strongest results come from human-AI collaboration](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12888660/) , where technology helps identify key findings while pathologists apply clinical judgment and expertise.


**Benefits beyond turnaround time**


While reducing turnaround time is often the primary objective, AI pre-screening can create value across multiple areas of laboratory performance:


- **Fewer unnecessary IHC stains** , helping reduce reagent consumption and laboratory costs
- **Greater pathologist efficiency** , enabling specialists to focus on complex or high-priority cases
- **Improved diagnostic confidence** , particularly among less experienced pathologists
- **Better workload management** , supporting laboratories facing workforce shortages and growing case volumes


These advantages make AI pre-screening an increasingly attractive component of broader digital pathology strategies.


**Looking ahead**


As digital pathology adoption continues to expand, AI is moving beyond workflow support toward more advanced biomarker prediction and virtual IHC applications. Emerging models can estimate biomarker status directly from H&E slides and may eventually reduce reliance on certain physical staining workflows.


For laboratories evaluating digital transformation initiatives, AI-powered pre-screening represents a practical near-term opportunity. By automatically triaging negative cases, prioritizing suspicious findings, and helping optimize IHC utilization, AI has the potential to accelerate diagnostic workflows while preserving and enhancing the pathologist's central role in patient care.
